This kind of touches on my thesis about books written by philosophers, where various of the characters end up needing to represent various abstract concepts, such as "capitalism" in the case of this book as well as "interventionism." It makes for terrible literature, or worse terrible storytelling.

Necessarily, the whole thing becomes preachy. It took me a while to diagnose this particular problem, but preachy is the word for it. How couldn't it be preachy? Greek mythology, after all had (fictional?) characters that represented abstract qualities, but these characters end up with likeable (or unlikeable) quirks, with individual personalities. Philosophers such as Rand or Nietzsche fail to achieve this. They end up writing more about how they wish something like capitalism were, instead of how it ends up actually playing out. Uncomfortable merely expressing their feelings in the form of a poem, or something they strawman the heck out of the topic by making Intervention into an idiot, and Enterprise into a hero.
Likeable people don't set out to write like this, have enough empathy to understand that no one wants to read this sort of material, so we get Ayn Rand.
This is the libertarian crowd - they want to imagine that life is like the board game Monopoly, a capitalist adventure, and they're happy with the game as long as everyone is paying attention and as long as they're winning.
